lesson.subtitle: Lesson 12 -- The Rules of the Game
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Monaco | Lesson 12 -- The Rules of the Game

paras: Professional sport is not governed by the country it happens in. It is governed by a private pyramid of bodies — a national federation, a continental confederation, a world governing body — each of which writes its own rules, licenses its own officials and runs its own disciplinary machinery. An athlete who signs a contract in São Paulo agrees, somewhere in the small print, that a dispute about a two-year ban will not be heard by a Brazilian judge. It will be heard in Lausanne, by three arbitrators, under Swiss law. Most people who follow sport are said to have no idea this is the case until it happens to somebody they support.

The body at the top of that structure is the Court of Arbitration for Sport, which is commonly described as the supreme court of world sport and is, in strict terms, nothing of the kind. It is an arbitral tribunal: a private forum the parties have agreed in advance to use. Its awards are final, they are enforceable in almost every country, and they are handed down by lawyers rather than by anybody elected. It is often claimed that the arrangement exists to keep sport away from the courts. It is more accurate to say that it exists because sport is international and courts are not: a rule that means one thing in Madrid and another in Manchester is not a rule at all.

The price of that uniformity is paid in due process. Cases are heard quickly, often on paper, sometimes while the athlete is already serving a provisional suspension that will be counted back if the sanction is upheld and quietly forgotten if it is not. Evidence that would be argued over for a year in a criminal court is weighed in an afternoon. Athletes are routinely reported to have been cleared months after the season in which the result would have mattered, and nobody is thought to owe them anything for the difference. The standard of proof is lower than a criminal one, and it has to be, because an integrity unit cannot compel a bank in a country where it has no power at all.

What follows is a question any lawyer recognises immediately. If one body writes the rules, investigates the breach, prosecutes it and pays for the tribunal, what is left of the separation you would insist on anywhere else? Defenders of the system answer that consent cures it, because nobody is forced to turn professional. Critics answer that consent given at sixteen, in a contract nobody reads, to a monopoly with no competitor, is not the kind of consent a lawyer normally accepts. It is believed by a growing number of European courts that the second argument is stronger than sport has assumed, and the next decade is expected to test it.

listenings.text: People assume we exist to keep sport out of the courts, and that is not quite it. The reason is speed and the reason is uniformity. A player is transferred in July and the window shuts in September. A judge in one country will take three years to decide what a clause means, and by then the season it mattered in is history. So the parties agree in advance to come to us, and they agree that what we hand down is final. It is often said that the athlete has no real choice about that, and in practice the athlete does not. What I would say is that the choice was never between this tribunal and a perfect trial. It was between this tribunal and twenty-eight national answers to the same question, which is how you end up with a rule that means one thing in Madrid and another in Manchester.

The public picture of match-fixing is a brown envelope in a car park, and in eleven years I have never seen one. What we see is betting data. A market that moves at three in the morning, in a country with no interest in the match, on an outcome nobody would price that way, and it moves before anything at all has happened on the pitch. That is the alert. Then the slow part starts, and the slow part is where most files die, because the money is believed to have moved through four jurisdictions and we can compel disclosure in none of them. People are often reported to have been charged when what has actually happened is that they have been provisionally suspended while we ask questions. The difference matters enormously to them, and it is never in the headline.

extra_audio.text: An alert is raised, usually by data rather than by a person, and the governing body opens a file. The athlete is notified and, under most codes, provisionally suspended while the file is built. A hearing is held, on paper or in a room, and both sides put their case. A first-instance panel hands down a decision, and either a sanction is imposed or the athlete is cleared. And then, within twenty-one days, either side may take the whole thing to arbitration in Lausanne, where a final award is made and no ordinary court will reopen it.
